roadmap_tasks.title: Build GitHub Actions release pipeline with OIDC scoped tokens and two-stage prepare/approve flow
roadmap_tasks.implementation_note: Owner: release engineering + SRE. Removes maintainer-local token exposure; dry-run on a release candidate before cutover.

roadmap_tasks.title: Migrate PyPI and Docker Hub publishing to OIDC trusted publishers
roadmap_tasks.implementation_note: Owner: release engineering. Eliminates long-lived publishing secrets; must follow CI pipeline migration.

roadmap_tasks.title: Implement canary release, post-release artifact verification, and compromise runbook with game day
roadmap_tasks.implementation_note: Owner: SRE + security. Final resilience layer; game day simulates pyproject.toml tampering to validate detection and response.

remediations.dependency_notes: The critical path runs t1/t2/t3 in parallel during days 1–12 to immediately close the injection vector and remediate potential existing compromise, since these require no dependencies and directly address the RPN 162 risk. t4 (CI guards) depends on t2 because it reuses the semver validation logic and enforces it in CI. t5 (monitoring) depends on t4 because it alerts on the same guard signals and release-path events. t6 (CI release pipeline) is the major architectural change and depends on t1, t2, and t4 — the hooks must be safe and validated before the pipeline is built around them, and CI guards must exist so the pipeline can rely on them. t7 (OIDC publishing) depends on t6 because trusted publishing is configured within the new pipeline. t8 (canary, verification, runbook) is the final layer and depends on t5, t6, and t7, as it verifies artifacts produced by the new pipeline and exercises the monitoring in a game day.
remediations.rpn_priority_note: With RPN 162 (Medium priority but severity 9), the roadmap front-loads the cheap, immediately effective fixes (hook rewrite, version validation, token rotation) into days 1–12 to close the critical injection path, while deferring the heavier architectural migration (CI pipeline, OIDC, canary) to days 30–90 since those have longer lead times but reduce residual risk rather than closing the active vulnerability.

explanations.failure_mode: Default SECRET_KEY 'changeme' enables JWT forgery and full auth bypass in any deployment that doesn't rotate it
explanations.scenario_summary: A publicly known default signing key allows an attacker to forge valid JWTs and impersonate any user, staff member, or app on any deployment that fails to rotate it.
explanations.code_connection: The JWT validation in saleor/graphql/middleware.py trusts settings.SECRET_KEY for signature verification, and the default value 'changeme' is shipped in .devcontainer/backend.env and referenced in .env.example — there is no startup check or warning that refuses to run with a known-default key in production.
explanations.links_to_other_scenarios: This is the same class of hardcoded-credential exposure as the populatedb admin/admin superuser and the devcontainer Postgres saleor/saleor credentials — all three rely on the operator remembering to rotate a publicly documented default, and a forged JWT from this scenario would grant the same superuser powers as logging in with the populatedb credentials.

explanations.failure_mode: populatedb creates superuser admin@example.com/admin with documented credentials — internet-exposed dev/staging instances are trivially compromised
explanations.scenario_summary: A management command creates a superuser with publicly documented credentials, so any network-reachable instance that ran it can be fully taken over with zero attacker effort.
explanations.code_connection: The populatedb command (referenced in CONTRIBUTING.md and pyproject.toml help text) hardcodes email admin@example.com and password 'admin' when --createsuperuser is passed, and there is no guard preventing this from running on a non-localhost deployment or warning that the credentials are public.
explanations.links_to_other_scenarios: This shares the hardcoded-default-credentials theme with the SECRET_KEY 'changeme' scenario, and a compromised staging instance here can pivot to production exactly as described in the devcontainer exposure scenario where local services share infrastructure with production.

explanations.failure_mode: Pre-commit local hooks execute manage.py (full app import) on developer machines during git commit — malicious PR code runs with reviewer's credentials
explanations.scenario_summary: Pre-commit hooks configured with language: system run ./manage.py on untrusted PR code, importing the full Django app and executing attacker-controlled module-level code with the reviewer's local credentials.
explanations.code_connection: The migrations-check hook (files: models\.py$) and gql-schema-check hook both invoke `sh -c './manage.py ...'` directly, and manage.py bootstraps the entire Django application — so any module-level code in an attacker-modified models.py or imported module executes during the commit, with no sandboxing or isolation.
explanations.links_to_other_scenarios: This is a supply-chain entry point that chains directly into the release-it command injection scenario: a malicious PR merged by a maintainer can modify pyproject.toml, and the same reviewer-credential theft here (GitHub tokens, SSH keys) is exactly what the release hook injection exfiltrates; it also shares the 'attacker-controlled code executes in a trusted context' pattern with the Semgrep bypass scenario where a malicious app runs in-process.

explanations.failure_mode: Semgrep no-requests-lib rule only blocks requests.* — urllib.request/http.client bypass the SSRF wrapper entirely, giving a false sense of SSRF coverage
explanations.scenario_summary: The static-analysis rule meant to enforce use of the SSRF-protected HTTPClient only matches the requests library, so any other HTTP client bypasses all SSRF protections while appearing compliant.
explanations.code_connection: The rule .semgrep/security/requests/no-use-requests-lib.yaml pattern-matches only requests.get/post/put/delete/head/patch/request and requests.Session(), while the project's own .claude/skills/filter-benchmark/analyze_query.py uses urllib.request.urlopen() to POST data — demonstrating the bypass exists in the codebase itself and passes CI cleanly.
explanations.links_to_other_scenarios: This validation gap is the same 'incomplete coverage gives false assurance' pattern as the filter-benchmark skill's unredacted explain.dalibo.com upload (a tool meant to help also leaks data), and the resulting SSRF to the cloud metadata endpoint is the delivery mechanism that would exploit the devcontainer's exposed, unauthenticated local services if an app runs on a developer machine.

explanations.failure_mode: Devcontainer exposes Postgres superuser and Valkey on host ports with hardcoded credentials — any local process gets full DB access
explanations.scenario_summary: Docker Compose maps Postgres (superuser saleor/saleor) and unauthenticated Valkey to host ports, so any process on the developer's machine gets full database superuser access with no additional conditions.
explanations.code_connection: docker-compose.yml maps port 5432 with POSTGRES_USER=saleor / POSTGRES_PASSWORD=saleor (superuser, not a limited role) and maps Valkey port 6379 with no password or auth configured — there is no network isolation, no non-superuser dev role, and no warning that these are host-exposed.
explanations.links_to_other_scenarios: This is the same hardcoded-credentials theme as SECRET_KEY 'changeme' and populatedb admin/admin, and it is the local execution environment that makes the pre-commit manage.py code-execution scenario and the Semgrep-bypass SSRF scenario directly exploitable on developer machines that often also hold production credentials.

explanations.failure_mode: filter-benchmark skill uploads full SQL query plans (with embedded data literals) to public third-party service explain.dalibo.com
explanations.scenario_summary: The benchmarking skill's analyze() function sends EXPLAIN ANALYZE output containing real query literals — potentially customer PII, gift card codes, and order data — to a public unauthenticated third-party service.
explanations.code_connection: In .claude/skills/filter-benchmark/analyze_query.py, _run_explain() executes EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, ..., FORMAT JSON) on the queryset's SQL with inlined parameter values, and the result is uploaded via urllib.request.urlopen() to https://explain.dalibo.com/new with no redaction of literal values, no opt-in consent, and no data processing agreement — the same urllib.request call that the Semgrep no-requests-lib rule fails to flag.
explanations.links_to_other_scenarios: This scenario is a direct instance of the Semgrep urllib.request bypass (the upload call itself evades the SSRF rule) and compounds the devcontainer exposure scenario: a developer benchmarking against a staging database reachable from the exposed local Postgres port can leak that data to a public service, turning a local misconfiguration into a GDPR-relevant third-party disclosure.

explanations.failure_mode: release-it hooks interpolate pyproject.toml version into shell commands — command injection during release gives attacker the maintainer's GitHub token and push access
explanations.scenario_summary: The release process interpolates the version string from pyproject.toml unquoted into shell commands, so anyone who can modify that file can inject commands that run with the maintainer's GitHub token and push access during a release.
explanations.code_connection: The after:bump and after:release hooks in the release-it configuration run `git checkout -B release-${version} --track`, `git push origin release-${version}`, and `gh pr create ... --title "Release ${version}"` with the version taken verbatim from pyproject.toml and no shell quoting or sanitization — a version containing metacharacters executes arbitrary shell in the maintainer's environment.
explanations.links_to_other_scenarios: This is the highest-impact link in the chain: the pre-commit manage.py scenario provides the initial code-execution vector on a maintainer's machine, and a malicious merged PR can modify pyproject.toml so that the next `npm run release` exfiltrates the maintainer's GH_TOKEN — the same credential theft that the pre-commit scenario describes — enabling a full supply-chain compromise of the repository and all downstream Saleor deployments.

scenario_linkage.cross_cutting_themes: The scenarios cluster around four recurring themes: (1) hardcoded or default credentials shipped in the repo (SECRET_KEY 'changeme', populatedb admin/admin, Postgres saleor/saleor, unauthenticated Valkey) that are publicly documented and rely on operators rotating them; (2) untrusted code execution in trusted contexts — pre-commit hooks importing attacker-controlled Django code with reviewer credentials, release-it shell injection with maintainer tokens, and malicious apps running in-process — forming a supply-chain chain from PR to production release; (3) incomplete security controls giving false assurance — the Semgrep rule that only blocks requests.* while the project's own code uses urllib.request, and the filter-benchmark tool that leaks sensitive data to a public service while appearing to be a safe dev aid; and (4) environment exposure — devcontainer services mapped to host ports with superuser/no-auth access, which turns local developer machines into pivot points toward staging and production. Notably, several scenarios interlock: the Semgrep bypass is demonstrated by the filter-benchmark skill's own urllib upload, the pre-commit code execution enables the release-it injection, and the shared default-credential pattern means one forgotten rotation compromises authentication, databases, and local infrastructure simultaneously.

validations.failure_mode: Default SECRET_KEY 'changeme' enables JWT forgery and full auth bypass in any deployment that doesn't rotate it
challenges: Occurrence of 6 is under-scored: this is a credential/auth failure with a publicly known default value — automated scanners and botnets probe for exactly this pattern continuously. For an e-commerce platform handling daily customer transactions, occurrence should be 8-9, not 6.

Detection of 8 is over-scored: if the deployment is compromised via forged JWTs, there is no 'detection' of the root cause (default key) — the attack succeeds silently. However, the question is whether the *failure mode* (using default key) is detectable pre-harm. A startup check or config validation would catch this trivially, but none exists. The score of 8 reflects 'no pre-harm detection exists,' which is accurate, but the framing conflates 'no detection of misconfiguration' with 'no detection of attack.' The real issue is that occurrence is higher than scored.

Severity of 10 is correct but the rationale is incomplete: beyond direct data compromise, this enables lateral movement into payment processors, email systems (via app tokens), and cloud storage — the blast radius description captures this, but severity should explicitly note that auth bypass in a multi-tenant SaaS e-commerce platform is business-stopping.
validations.verdict: Critical and correctly prioritized, but occurrence is significantly under-scored for a publicly known default credential in a daily-transaction e-commerce platform — this is actively scanned for by automated attackers.

validations.failure_mode: populatedb creates superuser admin@example.com/admin with documented credentials — internet-exposed dev/staging instances are trivially compromised
challenges: Occurrence of 6 is over-scored: this requires a specific precondition — a dev/staging instance exposed to the internet. Most developers run this locally or on properly firewalled staging. The 'documented credentials' aspect is real, but the exposure condition is not the default state. Occurrence should be 4-5, reflecting that internet-exposed staging is common but not universal.

Severity of 9 is over-scored for the typical case: compromise of a dev/staging instance is serious, but the direct business impact is limited unless staging shares infrastructure with production. The 'lateral movement to production' is speculative — it depends on shared credentials, network segments, or secrets, which is not guaranteed. Severity of 7-8 better reflects the realistic worst case without assuming worst-case infrastructure coupling.

Detection of 6 is reasonable but could be lower (easier to detect): failed login attempts with known credentials would trigger standard auth monitoring, and the credentials are so well-known that they appear in threat intelligence feeds. However, many dev/staging environments lack monitoring, so 6 is defensible.
validations.verdict: Realistic supply-chain-adjacent risk, but both severity and occurrence are over-scored by assuming internet exposure and production coupling that are not default conditions.

validations.failure_mode: Pre-commit local hooks execute manage.py (full app import) on developer machines during git commit — malicious PR code runs with reviewer's credentials
challenges: Occurrence of 5 is over-scored: this requires a maintainer to (1) review and checkout an attacker's PR, (2) run git commit locally, and (3) the attacker's code must survive code review enough to be checked out. GitHub's PR review workflow typically involves CI checks first; a malicious models.py change would likely be caught or at least scrutinized. The social engineering bar is high for a well-known open-source project with maintainer review.

Severity of 8 is under-scored: this is a supply-chain attack on the *maintainers of a widely-used e-commerce platform*. Stolen GitHub tokens enable pushing to main, which propagates to all Saleor Cloud customers and self-hosted deployments. This is not just 'reviewer's machine' — it's the entire downstream ecosystem. Severity should be 9-10, comparable to the release-it injection (index 6) which scores 9.

Detection of 7 is over-scored: there is no pre-harm detection for this. The malicious code executes during import — by the time anything is 'detected,' the credentials are already stolen. Detection should be 9-10 (essentially undetectable pre-harm). The score of 7 incorrectly suggests some detection capability exists.
validations.verdict: Realistic and severe supply-chain vector, but occurrence is over-scored (high social engineering bar) while severity is under-scored (ecosystem-wide impact) and detection is significantly under-scored (no pre-harm detection exists).

validations.failure_mode: Semgrep no-requests-lib rule only blocks requests.* — urllib.request/http.client bypass the SSRF wrapper entirely, giving a false sense of SSRF coverage
challenges: Occurrence of 5 is over-scored: this requires a malicious Saleor App to be installed (which requires admin approval) or a vulnerability in core code to use urllib.request. The project's own code demonstrates the bypass exists, but there's no evidence of active exploitation. The 'false sense of security' is a real risk, but the actual occurrence of an attacker exploiting this specific gap is lower than 5 — more like 3-4.
Severity of 8 is correct: SSRF to cloud metadata endpoint leading to IAM credential theft is a well-established critical pattern. The blast radius to entire cloud account is accurate.

Detection of 7 is under-scored: this is a *static analysis gap*, not a runtime detection gap. The semgrep rule passes the code, CI passes, and there's no runtime SSRF detection mentioned. The 'detection' here is really 'the security control fails to catch the vulnerability' — which means detection of the *attack* is also poor. However, the framing is about the failure mode (incomplete semgrep rule), and detecting that the rule is incomplete requires security expertise. Detection of 7 is defensible but could be 8 given no runtime SSRF monitoring is described.
validations.verdict: Realistic security control gap with severe potential impact, but occurrence is over-scored — exploitation requires a malicious app or core vulnerability, not just the semgrep gap existing.

validations.failure_mode: Devcontainer exposes Postgres superuser and Valkey on host ports with hardcoded credentials — any local process gets full DB access
challenges: Severity of 7 is correctly calibrated: this is a developer-machine risk, not a production risk. The 'potential host compromise via Postgres privilege escalation' is real but requires additional conditions (specific Postgres version, extension availability). The primary impact is local data theft and potential staging/production pivot if the developer has those credentials.

Occurrence of 6 is correctly calibrated: devcontainers are commonly run, and any local process can connect. The 'any local process' condition is broad — malware, compromised npm packages, and malicious dev tools are common. This is a realistic attack surface for developer machines.

Detection of 5 is correctly calibrated: the exposure is by design (documented in devcontainer.json), so it's 'detectable' in the sense that it's visible in configuration. However, there's no alerting for unauthorized connections. The score reflects that this is a known, accepted dev-environment risk rather than a hidden vulnerability.
validations.verdict: Well-calibrated entry — realistic developer-environment risk with appropriate severity, occurrence, and detection scores reflecting the local-only blast radius and known configuration.

validations.failure_mode: filter-benchmark skill uploads full SQL query plans (with embedded data literals) to public third-party service explain.dalibo.com
challenges: Severity of 6 is under-scored: this is a GDPR violation involving unauthorized transfer of personal data to a third party without a data processing agreement. For a platform handling customer PII, regulatory penalties (up to 4% of global revenue under GDPR) and reputational damage are severe. Additionally, gift card codes or checkout tokens in query literals could enable direct financial fraud. Severity should be 7-8.

Occurrence of 4 is correctly calibrated: this requires a developer to (1) use the filter-benchmark skill, (2) run it against a database with real PII, and (3) not notice or care about the upload. This is a plausible but not universal scenario — the skill is a niche tool, and developers may use it on anonymized data.

Detection of 7 is over-scored: there is no detection of this data exfiltration. The upload happens silently, the URL is returned but not logged centrally, and there's no alerting. Detection should be 9-10 — the data leaves the organization with no visibility. The score of 7 incorrectly suggests some detection capability exists.
validations.verdict: Realistic privacy/compliance risk with under-scored severity (GDPR implications) and significantly under-scored detection (silent exfiltration with no monitoring).

validations.failure_mode: release-it hooks interpolate pyproject.toml version into shell commands — command injection during release gives attacker the maintainer's GitHub token and push access
challenges: Occurrence of 3 is correctly calibrated: this requires a multi-step attack chain — attacker modifies pyproject.toml (via malicious PR, compromised dependency, or pre-commit hook), maintainer merges/approves it, and maintainer runs release. Each step has friction. The version string must also survive release-it's own version parsing. This is a low-probability but high-impact scenario.

Severity of 9 is correctly calibrated: supply-chain compromise of a widely-used e-commerce platform, propagating to all cloud and self-hosted customers. This is comparable to the pre-commit hook attack (index 2) but with a different entry point.

Detection of 6 is under-scored: there is no pre-harm detection for this. The shell injection executes during the release process — by the time anything is 'detected,' the GitHub token is already exfiltrated. The release process is a trusted, infrequent operation with no security monitoring. Detection should be 8-9. The score of 6 incorrectly suggests some detection capability exists during the release workflow.
validations.verdict: Correctly prioritized as a high-impact supply-chain risk, but detection is significantly under-scored — the release process has no security monitoring and the injection executes silently with credential exfiltration.
